--- title: "ROC curve and AUC" description: "Measuring how well a model ranks positives above negatives, across all thresholds." --- **Question answered:** does the model rank policies with a claim above policies without one? ## Every threshold at once On the [previous page](confusion-matrix.qmd), each threshold gave one confusion matrix and with it one pair of rates: - the **true positive rate** (TPR, recall): the share of claims we flag, and - the **false positive rate** (FPR): the share of non-claims we flag. The **ROC curve** (receiver operating characteristic) plots this pair for every possible threshold. A very high threshold flags nothing: the curve starts at (0, 0). Lowering it flags more and more policies until everything is flagged, at (1, 1). The marked points are the thresholds from the previous page: ::: {#cell-fig-roc-gbm .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = plot_roc(y, {"GBM": b["GBM"]}, operating_points={"t = 0.2": ("GBM", 0.2), "t = 0.1": ("GBM", 0.1), "t = 0.05": ("GBM", 0.05)}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![ROC curve of the GBM, with three thresholds marked.](roc-auc_files/figure-html/fig-roc-gbm-output-1.png){#fig-roc-gbm width=424 height=417} ::: ::: The diagonal is a model that ranks at random: whatever share of policies it flags, it flags the same share of claims and non-claims. The further a curve bulges towards the top-left corner, the better the model ranks. ## Building the curve by hand Ten policies, sorted by predicted probability, make the construction concrete: ::: {#tbl-toy .cell tbl-cap='Ten toy policies and the ROC point after lowering the threshold to each score.' execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} toy_y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0]) toy_p = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.55, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1]) toy_roc = roc_points(toy_y, toy_p) toy_roc.assign(outcome=np.r_[np.nan, toy_y]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
threshold fpr tpr outcome
0 inf 0.000000 0.00 NaN
1 0.90 0.000000 0.25 1.0
2 0.80 0.000000 0.50 1.0
3 0.70 0.166667 0.50 0.0
4 0.60 0.166667 0.75 1.0
5 0.55 0.333333 0.75 0.0
6 0.50 0.500000 0.75 0.0
7 0.40 0.500000 1.00 1.0
8 0.30 0.666667 1.00 0.0
9 0.20 0.833333 1.00 0.0
10 0.10 1.000000 1.00 0.0
``` ::: ::: Each time the threshold passes a policy, the curve takes a step: **up** by 1/4 if it had a claim (4 positives), **right** by 1/6 if it didn't (6 negatives). A perfect model would go straight up first, then right. ::: {#cell-fig-toy-roc .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.2, 4)) ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=MUTED, linewidth=1) ax.fill_between(toy_roc["fpr"], toy_roc["tpr"], color=MODEL_COLORS["GLM"], alpha=0.1, linewidth=0) ax.plot(toy_roc["fpr"], toy_roc["tpr"], color=MODEL_COLORS["GLM"], marker="o", markersize=6, markeredgecolor="#fcfcfb", markeredgewidth=2) ax.set(xlabel="False positive rate", ylabel="True positive rate", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.02), aspect="equal") toy_auc = auc_trapezoid(toy_roc["fpr"], toy_roc["tpr"]) ax.annotate(f"AUC = {toy_auc:.3f}", (0.55, 0.3), color=INK_SECONDARY) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![ROC curve of the ten toy policies. Shaded: the area under the curve.](roc-auc_files/figure-html/fig-toy-roc-output-1.png){#fig-toy-roc width=421 height=413} ::: ::: ## AUC: two interpretations The **area under the ROC curve** (AUC) condenses the curve into one number between 0 and 1. It has two equivalent readings. **1. Geometric.** The area under the curve: 1.0 for a perfect model, 0.5 for random ranking (the diagonal). **2. Probabilistic.** The AUC is the probability that a randomly chosen policy *with* a claim gets a higher score than a randomly chosen policy *without* one (ties count half): $$ \text{AUC} = P\left(\hat p_i > \hat p_j \mid y_i = 1,\ y_j = 0\right). $$ The second reading makes clear that **AUC measures ranking only**. It's the Mann–Whitney U statistic, and it can be computed from ranks without drawing any curve. On the toy example, 20 of the 4 × 6 = 24 (claim, no-claim) pairs are ordered correctly: 20/24 = 0\.833. On the real test set, both computations agree, and so does a brute-force check that samples random pairs: ::: {#tbl-auc-check .cell tbl-cap='AUC of the GBM, computed three ways.' execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} rng = np.random.default_rng(1) p_pos = b.loc[y == 1, "GBM"].to_numpy() p_neg = b.loc[y == 0, "GBM"].to_numpy() i, j = rng.integers(len(p_pos), size=1_000_000), rng.integers(len(p_neg), size=1_000_000) sampled = np.mean(p_pos[i] > p_neg[j]) + 0.5 * np.mean(p_pos[i] == p_neg[j]) roc = roc_points(y, b["GBM"]) pd.Series({ "Area under the curve (trapezoids)": auc_trapezoid(roc["fpr"], roc["tpr"]), "Rank statistic (Mann–Whitney)": auc_rank(y, b["GBM"]), "1 million random pairs": sampled, }, name="AUC").round(4).to_frame() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
AUC
Area under the curve (trapezoids) 0.7127
Rank statistic (Mann–Whitney) 0.7127
1 million random pairs 0.7135
``` ::: ::: ### Gini coefficient Credit scoring and insurance usually report the **Gini coefficient** (also called the accuracy ratio or Somers' D) instead: $$ \text{Gini} = 2 \cdot \text{AUC} - 1. $$ It rescales AUC so that random ranking scores 0 and perfect ranking scores 1. The GBM's AUC of 0\.713 is a Gini of 0\.425. The insurance Gini computed from a Lorenz curve, which we'll meet with lift charts, is a close relative. ## Comparing the models ::: {#cell-fig-roc-compare .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = plot_roc(y, {m: b[m] for m in ("Null", "GLM", "GBM")}) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![ROC curves of all three models on the test set.](roc-auc_files/figure-html/fig-roc-compare-output-1.png){#fig-roc-compare width=424 height=417} ::: ::: The Null model gives everyone the same score, so its curve is the diagonal (AUC 0.5). The GBM (AUC 0\.713) ranks better than the GLM (AUC 0\.694). Its curve lies on or above the GLM's at 100% of false positive rates. Where one curve lies above another, that model is better *at every threshold* in that region. When curves cross, AUC alone hides which model is better in the region you actually operate in. How large is an AUC of 0.71? There is no universal scale. Whether a claim happens depends largely on chance, so even a perfect pricing model would be far from AUC 1. Judge AUC against the Null model, a simpler baseline and what is achievable for the problem, not against an absolute benchmark. ## What AUC does not tell you **It ignores calibration.** AUC depends only on the *order* of the predictions. Any transformation that keeps the order leaves it unchanged, even one that ruins the probabilities: ::: {#tbl-auc-calibration .cell tbl-cap='Order-preserving transformations of the GBM: same AUC, very different probabilities.' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"} variants = { "GBM": b["GBM"], "GBM / 10": b["GBM"] / 10, "GBM ^ 0.2": b["GBM"] ** 0.2, } pd.DataFrame({ "AUC": {k: auc_rank(y, v) for k, v in variants.items()}, "Average predicted probability": {k: v.mean() for k, v in variants.items()}, "Actual claim rate": {k: y.mean() for k in variants}, }).round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
AUC Average predicted probability Actual claim rate
GBM 0.713 0.037 0.037
GBM / 10 0.713 0.004 0.037
GBM ^ 0.2 0.713 0.492 0.037
``` ::: ::: All three rank equally well, but only the first predicts claim probabilities that resemble reality. If the probabilities themselves matter (pricing, expected cost, the threshold formula on the previous page), measure [**calibration**](calibration.qmd) as well. **It weighs all thresholds equally.** AUC averages over the whole curve, including regions no one would use. With 96% non-claims, a false positive rate of just 10% already means 16\,327 false alarms on the test set. If only the top few percent of scores will ever be acted on, look at the left part of the curve, at [precision–recall curves](precision-recall.qmd), or at lift charts. **It is an estimate.** The test set is a sample, so AUC has sampling uncertainty. Before concluding that the GBM beats the GLM, we need a confidence interval for the difference (bootstrap or DeLong's test, on a later page). ## Takeaways - The ROC curve shows the trade-off between catching positives (TPR) and false alarms (FPR) across **all thresholds**. - AUC is the **probability of ranking a random positive above a random negative**: 0.5 is random, 1.0 is perfect. Gini = 2·AUC − 1. - AUC measures **ranking only**: it says nothing about whether the probabilities are right. - Under heavy imbalance, complement it with precision–recall or lift, and always quantify its uncertainty when comparing models.
